title: Position limits
objectives: Manage inventory under a position limit.

screens.title: Room to buy
screens.prose: The interviewer has sold you 3 lots of the three-dice sum. Your desk allows 4 lots either way. Now they offer to sell you 2 more at your bid.
screens.question: How many lots can you buy without breaking the limit?

hints.text: How far is your point from the right end of the interval?
The interval ends at +4. You sit at +3.
Room to buy is $4 - 3 = 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Room to buy is the limit less your position.

byKey.ignored: You took the whole 2. That puts you at +5, over the limit.
byKey.sellroom: That is your room to sell, $4 + 3$. Buying moves you towards +4, not away.

explain.text: Room to buy is $4 - 3 = 1$, so you take 1 and refuse the second. Room to sell is $4 + 3 = 7$. A limit treats the two sides very differently once you hold a position.

screens.question: What do you show?

options.text: An offer only, such as 1 lot at 11

options.why: You kept the bid. One more fill on it takes you to +5, over the limit.

options.text: A bid only, to show you still like it
options.why: You quoted the side that adds to a long. A bid can only take you further over.
You stepped out. The offer reduces your risk, and the interviewer still wants a price.

hints.text: Which side of a trade would make you less long?
Selling reduces a long. Your offer is the side that sells.
Show the offer alone, priced to trade: 11 is just above fair.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. At the limit, only the side that reduces the position may trade.

byKey.both: You kept the bid. One more fill on it takes you to +5, over the limit.
byKey.none: You stepped out. The offer reduces your risk, and the interviewer still wants a price.

explain.text: At +4 a bid can only add, so you show the offer alone. Pricing it at 11, near fair, makes the sale likely. The app's game uses one size for both sides, so there you stop one fill short instead.

screens.title: The limit game
screens.prose: Eight turns on the three-dice sum, size 1 or 2, width 1 to 3. In this game one size covers both sides, so a one-sided quote is impossible. Stop one fill short. Once a fill would reach the limit, move that side more than £1 from fair, where nobody trades.
screens.question: Finish the eight turns with a P&L of at least £2 and no rule breaks.

schedule.text: A market on the sum of three dice, rolled at the end. Fair is £10.50. Your limit is 4 lots either way. Other traders deal only within £1 of fair.

hints.text: Which side keeps trading? Watch your position after each turn.
Other traders keep selling to you. At +3 a bid fill would take you to the limit.
Quote 9.5 at 11.5 for 1. Once you are long 3, drop the bid to 9 and keep the offer at 11.5.

feedback.correct: You finished inside the limit with edge on every fill.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the size at 1 and watch the room on the bid side.

byKey.low: Your P&L is under £2. Quote within £1 of fair so other traders deal with you.
byKey.crossed: Your bid met or passed your ask, so nobody traded. Keep the bid below the ask.
byKey.limit: A quote was larger than your room on one side. The fill had edge, but the limit comes first.
byKey.spread: Your width left 1 to 3. Keep the ask between 1 and 3 above the bid.

explain.text: The flow was one-sided: one buyer, then sellers. The model run bought 4 at 9.5 and sold 1 at 11.5, then dropped its bid to 9 at +3. It ended long 3 with +£3.50, and never touched the limit.

screens.title: What the limit saved
screens.prose: You finished at {{carry.lim.position|0}} lots, with a P&L in pounds of {{carry.lim.pnl|0}}. The table is the model run, settled at the roll $5 + 1 + 4 = 10$. Long 3 with cash of $-26.50$ is worth $-26.50 + 3 \times 10 = 3.50$.

state.caption: One lot a trade, P&L at the value 10. Turns 6 to 8: no trade.

screens.question: Had the roll been 7, what would the model run's P&L be, in pounds?

hints.text: The cash is fixed. Only the value of the 3 lots changes.
Long 3 at a value of 7 is worth 21.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the cash, −26.50, to 3 lots at 7.

byKey.old: You kept the value at 10. The roll changed.
byKey.sign: A long loses when the value falls. The sign is negative.
byKey.loss: That is the change, $-3 \times 3$. Add it to the +3.50 you had.

explain.text: Long 3, each lot loses 3 when the roll falls from 10 to 7: a swing of £9. At 4 lots the same roll costs £12. The limit caps how much one bad roll can take.

screens.title: Same bet, two bankrolls
screens.prose: A bet makes £10 on average, with a standard deviation of £100. One trader has £10,000 to lose. Another has £200.

state.caption: The shaded tail loses the whole £200 in one bet.

screens.question: Who should take the bet?

options.text: Both: the expected value is positive
options.why: You looked at the average alone. Two bad bets in a row end the £200 trader's game.

options.text: The trader with £200, who needs the gain more
options.why: You sized by need. A small bankroll can bear less risk, not more.

options.text: Neither: it can lose £100 or more
options.why: You looked at the risk alone. With £10,000 behind it, the bet is worth taking many times.

hints.text: Compare £200 with the bet's standard deviation.
£200 is only 2 sd of one bet.
The £10,000 trader can survive many bad bets and collect the edge. The £200 trader cannot.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each bankroll with the size of a bad outcome.

byKey.both: You looked at the average alone. Two bad bets in a row end the £200 trader's game.
byKey.small: You sized by need. A small bankroll can bear less risk, not more.

explain.text: If the outcomes are roughly normal, one bet loses more than £200 about 1.8% of the time, and a run of bad bets is far likelier. The £10,000 trader survives the swings and collects £10 a bet. Expected value says whether a bet is good; the bankroll says how much you can take.

screens.title: Bigger stakes, same edge
screens.prose: You start with £20 and stop at £0 or £40. Each bet wins with chance 0.55 at evens. Slide the stake and watch how many paths hit zero.
screens.question: Which stake gives the highest chance of ruin?

options.why: Many small bets let the edge work. Each bet is one step of a walk that drifts up.
£10 is risky, but one £20 bet leaves no room at all.

options.text: The chance is the same for every stake
options.why: The edge per bet is the same, but the number of bets is not. Fewer bets give the edge less time.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count how many losses in a row each stake survives.

byKey.s1: Many small bets let the edge work. Each bet is one step of a walk that drifts up.
byKey.same: The edge per bet is the same, but the number of bets is not. Fewer bets give the edge less time.

explain.text: By the gambler's ruin formula, £1 bets hit £0 1.8% of the time. £10 bets do so 40.1% of the time, and one £20 bet 45%. The edge never changed, only the bet against the bankroll.

screens.title: The growth curve
screens.prose: A new game. A coin lands your way with chance 0.6, paid at evens. You bet a fraction $f$ of your bankroll each time. The curve is the average log growth a bet. Drag the point to its peak.
screens.question: Drag the point to the fraction with the fastest growth.

hints.text: Move right while the curve still rises.
The curve flattens near a fifth of the bankroll.
The peak is at $f = 0.2$: growth 0.0201 a bet.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find where the curve stops rising.

byKey.high: You went past the peak. Betting more than 0.2 grows the bankroll more slowly, though each bet's average win is larger.

explain.text: Growth is highest at $f = 0.2$, where $g = 0.0201$ a bet. That is £20 of a £100 bankroll. Past it, the losses cost more in log terms than the wins add.

screens.title: Bet it all?
screens.prose: The interviewer says: "Each bet wins on average. Surely you stake as much as you can?" You have £100 and will make 50 such bets.
screens.question: What do you stake on the first bet?

options.text: £100: each bet has the most expected value
options.why: You maximised expected value per bet. One loss in 50 takes the bankroll to zero, and you lose at least once with near certainty.
You doubled the stake. At 0.4 the growth is −0.0024 a bet: the bankroll shrinks over time.
You stayed far below the peak. That is safe, but grows at less than half the Kelly rate.

hints.text: What happens to a full stake on the first loss?
Staking 1 means one loss leaves nothing. The curve falls past 0.2.
Stake the fraction where $g$ peaks: $0.2 \times 100 = 20$, so £20.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Size the bet by growth, not by the expected value of one bet.

byKey.all: You maximised expected value per bet. One loss in 50 takes the bankroll to zero, and you lose at least once with near certainty.
byKey.dbl: You doubled the stake. At 0.4 the growth is −0.0024 a bet: the bankroll shrinks over time.

explain.text: Expected value rises with the stake, but growth does not. Half Kelly grows at 0.0150 a bet, Kelly at 0.0201 and double Kelly at −0.0024. A full stake is ruined by the first loss.

screens.title: Fifty bets later
screens.prose: Stake 0.2 of the bankroll on each of 50 bets, from £100. The typical path grows by $e^{g}$ a bet, with $g = 0.020136$. In 50 bets the median path wins 30 and loses 20.
screens.question: What is the median bankroll after 50 bets, to the nearest pound?

hints.text: Growth adds up in logs: 50 bets give $50g$.

byKey.mean: You found the mean, $100 \times 1.04^{50}$. A few lucky paths pull it far above the typical one.
byKey.linear: You added $50g$ to 1 instead of raising $e$ to it. Growth compounds.

explain.text: The median path wins 30 times and loses 20: $100 \times 1.2^{30} \times 0.8^{20} = 273.68$. That equals $100 e^{50g}$, since $50g = 30\ln 1.2 + 20 \ln 0.8$. The mean, £711, is pulled up by rare paths.

screens.title: Sizing by risk
screens.prose:
Two rules size a position. A limit $L$ leaves room on each side:
$$\text{room to buy} = L - q, \qquad \text{room to sell} = L + q.$$
Kelly stakes a fraction of the bankroll, for a win of $b$ per £1 with chance $p$:
$$f^* = p - \frac{1 - p}{b}.$$
screens.question: A bet wins with chance 0.55 at evens. What fraction of the bankroll does Kelly stake?

hints.text: Put $p = 0.55$ and $b = 1$ into the formula.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $f^* = p - (1 - p)/b$.

byKey.p: You staked the win chance itself. Subtract the losing chance over the odds.
byKey.edge: You halved the edge. At evens, $f^*$ is the whole edge $p - q$, which is 0.1.

explain.text: At evens Kelly is $p - q = 0.55 - 0.45 = 0.1$, a tenth of the bankroll. Both rules cap risk by a measure of what you can bear. Kelly needs a win chance you can defend with numbers, not a feeling of being sure.

widget.solution:
import math
import random


def kelly_stake(p, b, bankroll):
    """Kelly stake in pounds for a bet that pays b per £1
    with win chance p. Never negative."""
    f = p - (1 - p) / b
    return max(0.0, f) * bankroll


def growth(p, b, f):
    """Average log growth a bet when staking fraction f."""
    return p * math.log(1 + b * f) + (1 - p) * math.log(1 - f)


def ruin_sim(p, stake, start, target, trials, seed):
    """Share of trials that hit 0 before target, betting
    stake at evens, winning with chance p each bet.
    Use rng = random.Random(seed) and rng.random() < p."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    ruined = 0
    for _ in range(trials):
        x = start
        while 0 < x < target:
            x += stake if rng.random() < p else -stake
        ruined += x <= 0
    return ruined / trials
widget.how: Check runs 12 hidden tests. Kelly and growth must be exact; growth is rounded to 6 places. Each ruin share must sit within 0.03 of the exact chance (0.012 for £1 bets). The same seed must give the same share.

hints.text: At evens, a win adds `stake` and a loss takes it away.
Clamp a negative Kelly fraction to 0: you do not bet against an edge you do not have.
Loop while `0 < x < target`, and count the trials that end at or below 0.

feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Check the clamp in `kelly_stake` and the stopping rule in `ruin_sim`.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check that each `...` is replaced.

explain.text: `kelly_stake` is $\max(0, p - q/b)$ times the bankroll. `ruin_sim` plays the walk from the explore screen, settling near 0.45, 0.401 and 0.0178. The edge is the same in each; the stake decides the ruin.

screens.title: A desk's limits
screens.prose: A desk gives each trader a risk limit: the daily P&L may have a standard deviation of at most £40,000. One trader is very sure of a contract whose daily sd is £800 a lot. Another is mildly keen on one at £200 a lot.
screens.question: How many lots may the very sure trader hold?

hints.text: The limit is on risk, so divide by the risk of one lot.
One lot carries £800 of daily sd.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the risk limit by the sd of one lot.

byKey.other: That is the quieter contract's count, $40{,}000 / 200$. The sure trader's contract moves four times as much.
byKey.conviction: You added the two traders’ counts, 50 and 200. Each has its own £40,000 of risk, so $40{,}000 / 800 = 50$.

explain.text: The sure trader holds 50 lots and the keen one 200, the same £40,000 of risk. Desks size by risk because conviction is cheap to state and hard to check. In an interview, size the same way: by risk, not by confidence.

ideas: A limit $L$ leaves room $L - q$ to buy and $L + q$ to sell. At the limit, quote only the side that reduces.
A good bet can still ruin a small bankroll: size each bet against what you can lose.
Kelly stakes $f^* = p - (1 - p)/b$; at 0.6 and evens that is £20 of £100, and double Kelly shrinks.

formula.name: Kelly fraction
formula.note: $p$ the win chance, $b$ the win per £1 staked.

summary.trap: Staking the most because each bet has positive expected value. Growth peaks at $f^*$, and one loss ruins a full stake.

quiz.prose: Limit 5 lots either way. You are short 2.
quiz.question: How many lots can you sell?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Room to sell is $L + q$ with $q = -2$.

byKey.buyroom: That is your room to buy, $5 - (-2)$.
byKey.limit: You ignored the 2 you are already short.

explain.text: Short 2 means $q = -2$, so room to sell is $5 - 2 = 3$. Room to buy is 7. Being short uses up the selling side.

quiz.prose: A risk manager sets your limit on a contract to zero for the afternoon. You are long 2 lots.
quiz.question: What may you quote?

options.text: Only an offer, until you are flat; then nothing

options.why: You quoted as if nothing changed. Any bid fill adds to a position you must remove.
You quoted the side that adds to a long.

options.text: Nothing at all, and keep the 2 lots
options.why: You froze. A zero limit means you must reduce, so you offer the 2 lots out.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A limit of zero allows only trades that reduce the position.

byKey.both: You quoted as if nothing changed. Any bid fill adds to a position you must remove.
byKey.nothing: You froze. A zero limit means you must reduce, so you offer the 2 lots out.

explain.text: With a limit of zero you are over it while you hold anything. You may only sell, until flat. Once flat, every trade breaks the limit, so you quote nothing.

quiz.prose: A bet pays 2 to 1 and wins with chance 0.4. Your bankroll is £500.
quiz.question: What is the Kelly stake, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $f^* = p - (1 - p)/b$ with $b = 2$.

byKey.evens: You priced it at evens, where 0.4 has no edge. The odds are 2 to 1.
byKey.noq: You staked $p$ of the bankroll. Subtract $(1 - p)/b$.
byKey.edge: You staked the whole edge, 0.2 a pound. Kelly divides the edge by the odds, 2.

explain.text: $f^* = 0.4 - 0.6/2 = 0.1$, so stake $0.1 \times 500 = 50$ pounds. The odds give the edge: at 2 to 1 a 0.4 chance is worth $0.4 \times 2 - 0.6 = 0.2$ a pound. Kelly stakes the edge over the odds: $0.2/2 = 0.1$.

quiz.prose: Three dice, fair 10.5, limit 4. You are long 4, all bought at 9.5. The roll comes out 3.
quiz.question: What is your P&L, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each lot bought at 9.5 is worth 3.

byKey.sign: You are long, and the value fell. The P&L is negative.
byKey.fair: You used the fair value 10.5 as the price paid. You paid 9.5.

explain.text: Each lot loses $9.5 - 3 = 6.5$, and $4 \times 6.5 = 26$. Three is the lowest roll, so £26 is the worst case. The limit is what keeps that worst case known before you trade.
